claims.text: The low hardness of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is caused by high stacking-fault energy.
The low strength of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is caused by high stacking-fault energy.
High stacking-fault energy promotes facile dislocation glide in this alloy.
High stacking-fault energy suppresses deformation twinning in this alloy.
High stacking-fault energy hinders activation of precipitation strengthening in this alloy.
Facile dislocation glide produces high plasticity in the alloy.
Facile dislocation glide and the absence of additional strengthening mechanisms limit work hardening and resistance to plastic deformation.
The applicable starting material is equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a homogeneous, single-phase solid-solution state.
Room-temperature quasi-static deformation should increase the dislocation density relative to the undeformed starting state.
Room-temperature quasi-static deformation should produce few or no deformation twins.
Room-temperature quasi-static deformation should produce little or no nanoscale precipitation.
High stacking-fault energy facilitates dislocation glide with minimal cross-slip.
The uniform solid solution lacks sufficient nanoscale precipitates and twin boundaries to arrest dislocation motion.
The lack of effective barriers to dislocation motion limits hardness and strength.
Mechanical testing should show high ductility together with low yield strength and hardness.
The undeformed alloy is expected to have low dislocation density and no significant secondary phases.
At room temperature and quasi-static strain rates around 10^-3 s^-1 or lower, thermal effects and dynamic strain aging are minimized.
